title: Alibaba Just Hit a New 52-Week Low After a 16% Week. Is the Selling Overdone Before Earnings?

 Wiltone Asuncion • 4 minute read Reviewed by: Michael Douglass Last updated Nov 18, 2026 @bilalulker from Getty Images via Canva, @Mikhail Mishunin from Getty Images via Canva
 Key Takeaways
 Alibaba fell 15.6% in the past week to a new 52-week low as the U.S. moved to cut off Chinese companies’ access to AI chips in overseas data centers.
 The rule spares the recommendation systems behind Alibaba’s shopping apps but targets the rented Nvidia computing its AI cloud uses.
 At about 11x forward earnings, the selling looks overdone, though analysts’ estimates predate the rule and the Nov. 19 report has to show cloud growth holding up.
 Alibaba ( BABA ) has fallen 15.6% in the past week, closing at a new 52-week low of $86.65 on Nov. 17, two days before it reports. Washington turned a reported chip rule into a real one, targeting the Nvidia ( NVDA ) computing Alibaba reportedly rents abroad.
 Washington made it official
 On Nov. 9, the Financial Times reported that Alibaba is the biggest client of Megaspeed, a Singapore firm that rents out Nvidia computing. The New York Times has linked a former Megaspeed executive to the scandal around Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12, and Megaspeed denies wrongdoing. Late on Nov. 11, The Information reported that the Commerce Department was finalizing a rule to stop Chinese companies from using advanced AI chips abroad, and Alibaba sank 7% the next day .
 On Nov. 16, Commerce issued an interim final rule: exporters now need a license to ship advanced chips to data centers anywhere that sell large amounts of computing to China-headquartered companies, and to ship them to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Existing data centers get 90 days to obtain licenses. Computing for commercial recommendation systems, like ranking products in e-commerce, is exempt.
 David Riedel, founder and president of Riedel Research, said on CNBC’s Closing Bell : “I don’t think it has a huge impact on NVIDIA’s business… But for the Chinese, for Alibaba in particular, it’s very bad.”

 The cloud needs chips it can’t buy
 AI Cloud and Compute Services revenue rose 45% in the June quarter, and CEO Eddie Wu said on the August call that “our AI and cloud revenue growth will accelerate further in the coming quarters.” He tied that to more supply . Capex rose 75% to RMB 67.7 billion that quarter, and free cash flow was an outflow of RMB 44.7 billion. Alibaba’s own T-Head chips are the hedge, but Wu said in March that they still lag foreign rivals.
 Cheap, but the estimates came first
 Analysts expect normalized EPS to rebound 65% in fiscal 2027 (the year to March 2027):
 Alibaba Group Holding (BABA): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to March) ( TIKR ) 
 Those estimates predate the rule, and some may come down.
 Still, Alibaba trades at about 11x forward earnings, below its five-year average of 13x:
 Alibaba (BABA): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years ( TIKR ) 
 The selling looks bigger than the rule justifies. The rule exempts the recommendation systems behind the shopping business, and China e-commerce earned RMB 107.5 billion of adjusted EBITA in fiscal 2026, more than the whole group’s RMB 76.4 billion. Nov. 19 is the test: cloud growth of 45% or better and a cloud margin above June’s 11.6% would show the chip squeeze isn’t biting yet. The rule is also interim, and data-center operators still have to enforce it by vetting their customers.
